content.english: I first met Shawn Lichaa of the Karaite Jews of America years ago while undertaking research for my master’s thesis, which looked at issues of gender, marriage and social change among the Karaite Jews of Cairo during the years 1945-1951. I later wrote a second thesis, which focused on the experiences of Karaite men imprisoned in Egypt during the 1967 war. During another trip to the USA, I had the pleasure of visiting Congregation B’nai Israel and meeting members of the Karaite community of Daly City, who spoke to me about their lives in Egypt and their move to the USA.

While working on this research I spent a great deal of time with the magazine {{em:al-Kalim}}, which was published by the Karaite Jewish community in Cairo during the 1940s and 50s. The Arabic word{{em:kalim}} is an epithet of the prophet Moses—{{em:Musa kalim Allah}} is “the one who spoke with God”—as well as meaning “speaker” or “spokesperson,” which made it an apt name for a publication that functioned as the mouthpiece of a Jewish community. When I was visiting Daly City I was dismayed to discover that many younger Karaites did not read Arabic and could therefore not access the wealth of information about their community that was contained in {{em:al-Kalim}}. I was delighted when Shawn later approached me to translate selections from the periodical for publication by The Karaite Press.

{{em:Al-Kalim}} first appeared in February 1945 and published twice monthly, apart from summer breaks, until it tailed off and finally folded in 1956. Although we do not have circulation figures, the magazine appears to have been remarkably successful, in that it outlived Egypt’s other Jewish publications by years, and was one of the longest-running Jewish publications overall.{{fn:1}} It was published by a community organisation named {{em:Jamʿiyyat al-shubban al-Israʾiliyyin al-Qarraʾin}} (The Young Men’s Karaite Jewish Association) and the editorial policy seems to have been inclusive; Karaite historian Mourad El-Kodsi recalls that the magazine would accept any submission “as long as it met the requirements of a worthwhile contribution.”{{fn:2}} Most of those who wrote for the publication were men, but occasionally women did too. Perusing the magazine thus provides a glimpse into the thoughts and opinions of a wide range of both committed writers and sometime contributors.
content.comments:
[1] Reuven Snir, “‘Mosaic Arabs’ between Total and Conditioned Arabization: The participation of Jews in Arabic press and journalism in Muslim societies during the nineteenth and twentieth centuries,” {{em:Journal of Muslim Minority Affairs}}27, no. 2 (2007): 261-295.

[2] Mourad El-Kodsi, {{em:The Karaite Jews of Egypt, 1882-1986}} (Lyons, NY: Wilprint, 1987, 2nd ed. 2006): 238.

content.english: {{em:Al-Kalim}} was largely preoccupied with Karaite affairs. Its pages featured regular updates on the state of the community’s synagogues and other properties, reminders to members to pay their {{em:ʿarikhah}} (subscription fee), and notices of births, engagements, marriages and deaths on its {{em:Akhbar rasmiyyah}} (official news) page, sometimes alongside photos of society weddings and other events. Once a year, the magazine printed the community’s annual report, with editorial commentary, as well as annual reports of the community’s charitable association {{em:Jamʿiyat musaʿadat al-faqirat ʿala al-zawaj}}(The Association to Assist Poor Women in Marrying).

Much of the magazine’s coverage was devoted to Karaite communal politics. Elections for the {{em:majlis milli}}(communal council) were announced in {{em:al-Kalim}}, centrefold spreads were given to the candidates and their platforms, and short write-ups of {{em:majlis}}business appeared regularly in the {{em:Akhbar mutanawwi}}ʿ{{em:ah}}(various news) section. Moreover, writers often criticised the {{em:majlis milli}}on a range of topics. Indeed, the magazine appears to have acted as a mouthpiece for the views of a group who were discontented with what they saw as a slow-moving, opaque, and perhaps outdated institution.

But politics and current affairs were by no means {{em:al-Kalim}}’s staple content. Articles on Jewish history, religious practices and holy texts appeared in virtually every issue, and the {{em:Hakham Akbar}}or Grand Hakham Tubiyah Simhah Lifi Babufitsh (Toviyyah ben Simhah Levi Babovitch) regularly contributed interviews or essays. The magazine also featured educational articles with an Egyptian or Jewish slant, or both—with titles like “The Traces of Pharaonic Civilisation in our Life Today,” and “The ‘Fidelity of the Nile’ Festival and the Influence of the Karaites on its Celebration During the 19th Century”—alongside more general educational pieces about science, history, and geography.

Every issue contained a section entitled {{em:Hadiqat al-adab}}(garden of literature) featuring both standard Arabic {{em:qasa}}ʾ{{em:id}}(odes) and vernacular Egyptian {{em:azjal}}(strophic poems written or performed in dialect), as well as short stories of a page or two in length, reflecting the great extent to which the Karaites shared the traditional, as well as the newer and more experimental, forms of cultural expression current in their Arab and Egyptian environment. There were lighter items, too: many issues featured a page of jokes and caricatures, and {{em:al-Kalim}} ran “most beautiful baby” competitions which saw a page of each issue devoted to photos of the adorable chubby-cheeked competitors.

Writers often contributed comment pieces on social issues such as marriage, divorce, gambling, poverty, and the role of women. Numerous articles discussed, for example, the problem of poverty and the need for better welfare mechanisms, usually conceived of as charitable institutions to which richer members of the community would be duty-bound to contribute. Indeed, communal institutions—from sports clubs and soup kitchens right up to hospitals—were almost always proposed as the most effective vehicle for addressing the needs of the community. Writers frequently compared their own community with the Rabbanite Jews—respectfully referred to throughout as “our brothers”—bemoaning the Karaites’ inability to sustain communal institutions or welfare projects as successfully as the Rabbanites, or noting innovations that the Rabbanites had come up with. Occasionally, tensions arose from the Karaites’ ambiguous relationship with the larger Rabbanite community, which was better served by communal institutions (it had far more schools, for example, and ran the Jewish hospital) and often provided services to the Karaites too. In 1951, for example, one contributor was outraged at the decision by the director of the Rabbanite schools to exclude Karaite children from that year’s summer excursions.

Writers often stressed the importance of the Karaites’ reputation in support of their views. This may have been linked to the heightened scrutiny to which all Jews were being subjected at the time as a consequence of Zionist activity, viewed with hostility by the Egyptian government (perhaps the removal of the tablets, with their Hebrew inscription, from the front cover of {{em:al-Kalim}} in autumn 1948, was also a result of this factor). It may also have reflected the fact that Egyptian society was still effectively organised along denominational lines, as it had been under the Ottoman millet system, and that communal identity and reputation were always at stake in any social debate. There was a hearty appetite for reform in certain areas—as we have seen, the secretive and undemocratic manner in which the {{em:majlis milli}}operated frequently provoked condemnation and calls for change—and mixed feelings in others. Writers expressed distinctly ambivalent views on divorce, for example: frequent contributor Ili Amin Lishaʿ in one article advised married couples that they should not hesitate to divorce if they felt it was necessary, yet in another article described divorce as ‘what God detests most of all He permits’ {{em:(abghad al-halal}}ʿ{{em:ind al-lah)}}. Lishaʿ’s phrasing highlights another important feature of these articles, namely that writers frequently marshalled religious arguments—usually Jewish, often specifically Karaite, and sometimes also Islamic—in support of their views.

The Karaite community by and large remained in Egypt much longer than the country’s other Jews. Nevertheless, a series of dire events had a destabilising effect on Jewish life from the mid-1950s onwards. In 1954, a number of Egyptian Jews were involved in a botched Israeli bombing campaign codenamed Operation Susannah, and one of them—Musa Marzuq, better known as Moshe Marzouk—was a Karaite Jew. Marzuq was executed in January 1955, but the incendiary affair was not covered in {{em:al-Kalim.}} The magazine ran throughout 1955 then appeared only a handful of times in 1956; the issue which would prove to be its last was published on August 15 of that year. The same year brought the Suez Crisis or Tripartite Aggression, which increased the pressure on Egypt’s remaining Jews, yet many Karaites remained in Egypt for another decade. The final blow to the community came with the Egyptian government’s decision to imprison Jewish males of military age during the Six Day War, and for several years afterwards. Many of the Karaite internees and their families left the country en masse in 1970 after the Egyptian government agreed to release the imprisoned Jews on the condition they emigrated immediately and renounced their Egyptian citizenship. Since {{em:al-Kalim}} was long gone by this time, we have little written evidence of how the community experienced and viewed these events. Nonetheless, it is important not to project the rapid and tragic decline onto earlier years of Karaite life in Egypt. In 1953, the community was contemplating building a new synagogue in Cairo’s affluent Heliopolis district, where many Karaites then lived (see {{em:The Heliopolis Synagogue}}), and even in January 1956, an article describes how the Egyptian government viewed Zionism as colonialism, but pledged its ongoing support for Egypt’s Jews (see {{em:Egypt’s Jews Receive Support From the Revolution}}).

The many names and terms which appear in these texts reflect the rich and diverse religious, cultural and intellectual world of the Egyptian Karaite Jews, which included Arabic, Hebrew, Slavic, and European elements. For the sake of consistency, and to reflect the pre-eminence of Arabic in Egyptian Karaite life, I have in most cases transliterated directly from Arabic using the International Journal of Middle East Studies system without diacritics. This may at times result in unfamiliar spellings: thus the name commonly spelled Menashe is given here as Minashsha, Levi as Lifi, Elie as Ili, and Itzhak or Yitzhak as Ishaq; the Slavic surname of the {{em:Hakham Akbar}} who hailed from Crimea is transliterated as Babufitsh; European names appear in their Arabized versions, for example Léonie as Liyuni. The authors of individual articles are listed in the translation wherever they are listed in the original. Often, general interest pieces were not credited to a specific author.

With its wide-ranging subject matter, {{em:al-Kalim}} is a compendious resource for the study of the Karaites in Egypt during the 1940s and ’50s. For readers who remember those times, I hope this book will bring back good memories, and for those who do not, I trust it will be an enjoyable glimpse into a significant and fascinating period in the life of the Egyptian Karaite community.

paragraphs.english: The trip everyone’s waiting for—organised by the Young Men’s Karaite Jewish Association in Egypt.
It gives the Association great pleasure to inform members of the community that it has organised this trip to assist them in performing the rites of pilgrimage on the holy holiday of Shavuʾot.
The trip, God willing, will begin in Cairo on Monday 14th May 1945, returning Sunday 27th May according to the planned schedule.

The cost of the trip per person will be 40 Egyptian pounds, covering the cost of transportation, rail fares (second class), accommodation and board in respectable guesthouses (second class), visits, and the cost of travel permits.
The necessary arrangements have been made with the travel agency organising the trip to ensure the provision of kosher meat slaughtered according to our custom.
The deadline for reservations is the end of February 1945. Reservations must be accompanied by a deposit of 10 Egyptian pounds per person.
Please note that the number of places is limited and will not be exceeded, likewise the number of travel permits. Early reservation and payment of deposit is therefore recommended.
Reservations may be made using the relevant form and presented to the Association at its centre or to the representative at the {{em:hakhamkhanah}}{{fn:3}}, on any afternoon.
paragraphs.comments: [3] The administrative and religious office of the community.

paragraphs.english: Reservations must be accompanied, as far as possible, by the following documents: birth certificate, draft certificate, certificate from place of employment, passport, five photos.
Where a family is to travel together, a single passport will be obtained and the fees of the wife and children’s personal passports refunded to them.

articles.title: Reflections on the Days of the Week

paragraphs.english: {{em:Sunday:}}

I went out to work, in al-Sagha,{{fn:4}} and as I was opening up my store I was greeted by my neighbor, who told me that the price of gold had “{{em:ʿafshar ʿawi,}}” that is, fallen steeply, and that he didn’t know whether he should buy or sell. He said he was fed up with this business, which didn’t depend on a natural commodity that was consumed and subject to the law of supply and demand, but was affected by all sorts of factors which changed from one day to the next. I replied that it was quite true, that the time had come for us to leave this trade for one of the new industries, and that we should support them with our efforts; it would be ideal if we joined forces and founded companies that would participate in the national economy and bring in profits for their shareholders. I spent the rest of the day similarly anxious and pensive, and I did not work at all other than to value some gold for customers who’d come to check what their jewellery was worth, but not to sell it—and certainly not to buy anything new, because they wanted the price to continue falling.
paragraphs.comments: [4] The goldsmiths’ district, located close to the Karaite neighborhood in Cairo.

paragraphs.english: {{em:Monday:}}

My wife asked me over breakfast what I’d like for lunch, so I told her the usual. She told me she hadn’t been able to buy meat the previous day, because the butcher—after the servant had already waited in line for three hours because it was so busy—had given him a lump of mutton that was almost all bone; she asked the servant to exchange it for another piece, but he came back with a refund, reporting that the butcher had said, “That’s all the meat there is, and whoever wants it can have it.” The disgraceful wretch! How long will we be at the mercy of these butchers?
{{em:Tuesday and Wednesday:}}

I couldn’t write these past two days, because the dinner table contained nothing but lentils and beans, and I’m a man who likes to sit down and write after a nice, varied meal. A good lunch assists in thinking and sound logic, and I’ve noticed that different kinds of food affect the diversity of my articles. Indeed, my finest articles were written after a lunch of {{em:goz wi-tom}}{{fn:5}} on a Friday evening, or stuffed chicken on a Saturday.
paragraphs.comments: [5] A dish of chicken, garlic and swiss chard, enjoyed by the Karaite Jews of Egypt, particularly on Shabbat because it could be served at room temperature.

paragraphs.english: {{em:Thursday:}}

I left the store at four because business was slow, and asked a friend, a lawyer, if he’d like to spend the rest of the afternoon with me. He suggested I join him at a family gathering to which he was invited, and assured me I’d be welcome; I accepted reluctantly, for I’d have preferred an evening in the company of my lawyer friend alone, conversing about whatever topics presented themselves. The gathering was in honor of Susu’s success in his secondary exams, but in fact this occasion was merely an opportunity, a pretext even, to get together with friends and acquaintances who like gambling at cards. Well, I was like a stranger in a foreign country at that gathering, hardly understanding a word they said: Jacques would say “Conquin,”{{fn:6}} and Yusif would say “Pass;” Marco would say “Bankroll,” and Esther would say “Aces full!” I observed intense emotion on the faces of the winners and losers. One flushed red at the thought of losing what he’d won, another was yellow with vexation, miserably trying to win back what he’d lost, and all smoked prodigiously until the air was intolerable. I am fed up with such gatherings. Time wasted, money lost, and life squandered.
{{em:Friday:}}

When I got home from work in the evening, my wife startled me, saying “You need to have a word with your son, he’s been pestering his sister all day, and he says he’s going to buy a slingshot—I’m worried he’ll hurt someone. And why didn’t you send any bones for stock today?” That’s the reception a work-weary husband gets from his wife! I know a wife’s duty is considerable: she must put on pretty clothes and greet her husband with a cheery face, then, after helping him out of his work clothes, bring him whatever food and drink he would like. The father then makes conversation with his children and wife, and they spend a pleasant evening which helps the exhausted husband relax and edifies the wife and children, whilst assuring the wife that her husband will not go out and spend the evening elsewhere—and where do husbands go if not the coffee shop? Sitting in coffee shops encourages gambling, so be responsible, women, and think of the consequences for you and your husbands.
{{em:Saturday:}}

At sunset I had a coffee and enjoyed my first cigarette of the day, since I don’t smoke on Shabbat. This is a good habit I have adopted, because, as well as the fact that religion prohibits kindling flames on Shabbat, forgoing smoking one day of the week gives the chest some respite, teaches the soul abstinence and the denial of pleasure and temptation, and strengthens one’s will and morals.

articles.title: Prayer of Thanks

paragraphs.english: His eminence the Hakham [Tubiyah Babufitsh] led a prayer of thanks in ʿAbbasiyyah synagogue on Saturday May 12th [1945], and gave a speech of which we reproduce an excerpt here:

The will of God, the just ruler, may He be glorified and exalted, decreed that war should break out across the world because of the ambitions of the human race, and the earth shook and kingdoms were razed to the ground. The flames of war have blazed across the earth for more than five years and thrown people of all languages into disarray, and many set out for the battlefield. So many millions have been killed, so many millions widowed or orphaned, so many millions left starving for want of a mouthful of bread, so many millions left shivering for want of clothes to cover their backs, wandering from place to place in search of shelter and refuge. Remember the terrible days when the enemy had reached the gates of our country. Remember the days of El Alamein, and remember how God almighty showed his mercy and the enemy turned on his heel before the fearless soldiers of the Allied forces.

We therefore deliver this special prayer of praise and thanks to God the supreme and almighty for his mercy, and the noble favors he bestows upon us. We implore Him to commend the souls of those fallen on the fields of battle to eternal rest; they departed this transient world in the selfless sacrifice of their lives for the good of their countries and the happiness of the human race. We beseech Him, the all-powerful and sublime, to embrace us in His mercy—we the wretched who, it has been ordained, shall live—and to see that war shall not return to the world, and to spread peace amongst the kingdoms on the east of the Earth, which are still at war. May He transform that peace into an eternal peace which reigns across the world, and make it the beginning of a golden age, as our prophets, peace be upon them, foretold: “And He shall judge among many peoples, and render decisions for mighty, distant nations; and they shall beat their swords into ploughshares, and their spears into pruning hooks: nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more” (Micah 4:3).

May we live under God’s care, in lasting peace and happiness and harmony with our brothers in our dear homeland, under the beneficence of our beloved peace-adoring sovereign, His Majesty King Faruq the First, may God protect him.

articles.cover_caption: On the cover: “The late {{em:Hakham}} Mushih al-Qudsi II”
articles.title: Five Minutes with Five Young Women

paragraphs.english: If the outings organised by the Young Men’s Association from time to time are a welcome chance to meet up with relatives and friends, they are certainly the only way for the two sexes to meet and get to know each other. Our social life still imposes restrictions upon us, and regressive attitudes are still prevalent in our community, to the point that I’ve never attended a single wedding where men and women were not separated. So I seized the chance of the trip to al-Qanatir last month to pose three questions to five young women, who responded frankly and astutely—encouraging me to take another bold step and ask permission to publish their photos, which they granted.
It gives me great pride, then, to record here the good sense, intelligence and propriety of young Karaite women.
The editor [Yusif Kamal]
Question 1. {{em:How can young Karaite women participate in raising the social standards of the community?}}
Question 2. {{em:What do you think of the dowry system, and how can it be remedied?}}
Question 3. {{em:What are the most important qualities in the young man you would like to marry?}}
{{center:ʾ. Qudsi{{fn:7}}}}
paragraphs.comments: [7] The first initial (an {{em:alif hamza}} in Arabic) could be any vowel.

paragraphs.english: 1. The young Karaite woman does not enjoy full freedom, for she is a prisoner of traditions; her family do not let her go out and participate in public life, which limits her social activism. The contribution which the community wishes for from young women, at least at the present time, therefore has narrow horizons, and is limited to teaching young women home management, needlework and knitting.

2. Not a bad question—I could write a book about it. If we want to properly consider this subject we must view it in light of ordinary circumstances rather than citing wartime conditions as a measure of the cost of living. In all cases, the resolution of this issue lies in the hands of young men, who ought to think realistically and deeply about marriage before embarking upon it, and make material considerations the last thing they think of—because wealth does not equal happiness.
3. Whatever a young woman’s ideal of a husband might be, it’s all down to fate. Nevertheless, the most important qualities I hope for are loyalty, integrity, and respect.
{{center:M. Masʿuda}}

1. I would like to participate as much as my time permits in serving my community, if only humbly. However, the scarcity of women’s activism and the lack of charitable associations or institutions, similar to the Red Crescent or Mabarrat Muhammad ʿAli, leave me without a way to contribute to raising the social standard of the community, and all that a young woman like me can do is sew or embroider part of a poor bride’s trousseau for free.

2. My opinion on the dowry is the same as that of any young woman: it does no honour to young men and it diminishes the community, for marriage amongst us is a commerce, and it’s the pound that talks. If a young woman has plenty of gold, offers of marriage pour in from all quarters; if she does not, she is left on the shelf until God brings her relief. Resolution of this issue lies in men’s hands, not in ours.
3. Self-sacrifice and loyalty; he should treat me with respect; educated; he should understand me, and I him.
{{center:R. Tawil}}

1. Woman is the prophet of mercy upon the earth, so I see the first duty of young Karaite women as being to occupy themselves with the health and social affairs of the community; to that end, there should be a women’s association bringing together virtuous girls and women to provide treatment and solace to the sick, to care for children, attend to their cleanliness and provide sterilised milk, and to offer a helping hand to mothers.

2. The dowry system is rubbish. No matter how intelligent or beautiful a young woman might be, if she has no wealth she must give up hope of making a happy marriage, because the groom’s first question is “How much have you got?” As I see it, the solution to this problem is for the man and woman to share the burden of the trousseau and household requisites according to their respective abilities.
3. Firstly, he mustn’t be a gambler, and secondly, he must be loyal and reliable; beyond that, I don’t mind whether he is rich or poor.
{{center:R. Lishaʿ}}

1. Spread the sporting spirit amongst the community’s young women by founding a scout troop, and found a club that would bring together young men and women so that women can work side by side with men; of course, this will not distract us from promoting prayer and a religious spirit. Young Karaite women will thus be healthy in body and strong in faith.

2. The dowry system contravenes religion, which stipulates that the man must pay the dower. The solution lies in a strike by fathers, who should refuse to pay dowries until young men eventually submit to the rule of religious law; but once this is the case, I don’t see any problem with a wealthy father of the bride assisting the young man with expenses.
3. A sporty young man, who is modern, has good etiquette, and knows how to love and respect me.
{{center:N. Sulayman}}

1. Man is of woman’s creation, so if you want great and virtuous men, you must teach women the meaning of greatness of soul and virtue. Young Karaite women must participate in promoting education and eradicating illiteracy amongst women and girls, for when women are educated they are able to assist men in bearing life’s burdens.

2. I disagree completely with the dowry system—should a young woman who is poor not be able to marry? The solution is for the groom to bear the costs if he is wealthy, and if he is not but the bride is, then she should contribute her wealth.
3. Above all, he mustn’t be a gambler or a drinker; he must be upstanding and educated, and know how to respect and value me.

articles.title: And the Mezuzah

paragraphs.english: God says in His precious book the Torah what I translate in letter and in spirit as follows: The commandment which I enjoin upon you this day is neither astonishing nor distant, for neither is it in the sky such that you might say, “Who will go to the sky for us and bring it to us?,” nor is it across the seas such that you might say, “Who will cross the seas and bring it to us, and recite it to us that we may do by it?” It is very close to you, so you may fulfil it with your tongue and your heart.{{fn:8}} Elsewhere, God—may He be glorified and exalted—says: I did not not speak in secret but before all.{{fn:9}} There is no confusion, then, no ambiguity or vagueness in His commandments.
paragraphs.comments:
[8] Deuteronomy 30: 11-14.

[9] Perhaps a paraphrase of Isaiah 45:19.

paragraphs.english: And if we trace the history of the sons of Israel from the time of their exodus from Egypt to the destruction of the Temple we see that God the all-powerful and sublime sent them prophets in preparation that he did not send to other nations, to guide them and straighten their deviation. They greeted the prophets with insults at times, and with disdain and shrugging of shoulders; none listened to the admonishments and counsel and warnings which God sent to them in the hands of His prophets. If for one day they were awake and right in their ways and worshipped God, then for many years it was not so, and they were turned over and failed to believe in God. Given what God—may He be glorified and exalted—had seen of their reticence, apostasy, idol-worship, unbelief and violation of His commandments in the days of their journey in the desert of Sinai, He wanted to guide them, capture their attention and remind them, in case the reminder should benefit{{fn:10}}: so he commanded them to remember God by way of {{em:Shemaʿ Yisraʾel}}{{fn:11}}, in all their comings and goings, at their falling asleep and their rising, and to recite it in their homes and repeat it to their children. And then God—may He be glorified and exalted—having put those people to the test and found that they were liable to deny Him and disobey His orders, wanted them to be constantly reminded and exhorted to fear and worship Him in all their movements and stillnesses. So, he commanded them to write {{em:Shemaʿ Yisraʾel}} on the posts of their doors so that upon crossing they would see it and remember God. This {{em:mezuzah}}was used in former times, but now, the people have recognised that God is truth, and there is no longer any need for it.
paragraphs.comments:
[10] This echoes Quranic phrasings such as “So remind, if the reminder should benefit” ({{em:fa-dhakkir in nafaʿat al-dhikra}}; 87:9) and “And remind, for indeed, thae reminder benefits the believers” ({{em:wa-dhakkir fa-inna al-dhikra tanfaʿ al-muʾminin;}} 51: 55). It is interesting that the author connects these Qurʾanic injunctions regarding reminders with God’s command to the Israelites to remember the {{em:Shemaʿ}}.

[11] In Hebrew in original.

paragraphs.english: In peace,
Yusif Ibrahim

articles.title: Determining Holiday Dates

paragraphs.english: Every year as the Hebrew New Year holiday approaches, clamour and controversy erupt amongst the men of religion in our community as to which exact day should be taken as the New Year holiday, and hence the other holidays too. As is well known, our holidays follow a calendar issued by {{em:Dar al-Sharʿ}}that is based on the calculations of the scholar Yehuda Kukizub [Kokizov], and our months proceed according to the lunar system. This year, a group of men of religion caused considerable contention by declaring that the holiday of the New Year should fall on the 26th September and not the 27th, as the calendar stated. They had verified this with the Office of Natural Sciences, which is followed by the Helwan Observatory, and submitted a confirmation from the Office that the moon had been sighted on the evening of the 25th, as a result of which fact the 26th was the first day of the Arabic month, and indeed our brothers celebrated on that day. There can be no doubt, given the confirmation of the moon sighting, that the first day of the Hebrew month fell on the 26th September—and if that is the case then we celebrated the New Year holiday, and indeed all of the holidays, incorrectly.

Despite the fact that those who contacted the Office of Natural Sciences notified {{em:Dar al-Sharʿ}} that the New Year holiday should be celebrated on the 26th, the latter took no steps to announce as much to the community and instead left them to flounder in confusion, with some saying the holiday would fall on the 26th, and others the 27th.

We should now like to know if the intention is to uphold the dates given in the calendar, despite the potential ramifications of calendrical divergence from the lunar cycle. Note that the Egyptian government publishes annually an almanac which is subject to adjustment if the moon is sighted outside of the times predicted. Each year on the eve of the first day of Ramadan, as we all know, an event takes place called the “celebration of the sighting”: if the moon is sighted, then the holiday is celebrated one day prior to the date advertised in the almanac, and the almanac ceases to be followed since the ultimate point of reference is the new moon. This is what the Egyptian government does; yet in our community when the new moon is sighted we go against the whole world by keeping to our calendar, making ourselves the subject of criticism by members of the other religions.

I know that it takes a day in order to announce the start of a new month, and likewise that the new moon must be sighted for a given amount of time. Nevertheless, on no occasion in years past have we adjusted the dates of our calendar based upon a sighting of the new moon for the specified amount of time.

I believe that the time has come to institute a committee whose task it is to check the dates specified for the holidays, and announce the results to members of the community in advance, so that we may celebrate our holidays on the correct dates rather than early or late, and so that we may not fall into confusion about our holidays at the start of each Hebrew year.
Ili Amin Lishaʿ

articles.cover_caption: On the cover: “Hypocrisy”
articles.title: The Dispute over Land in al-Basatin

paragraphs.english: We have written in {{em:al-Kalim}} on more than one occasion about the land in al-Basatin [cemetery] and the need to demarcate the area that belongs to us. We reported that our brothers have begun to bury their dead within our section of land, in response to which the communal council has looked into the matter and been in contact with our brothers’ council. The essence of the disagreement is that they wish to take over the area of land on the boundary, which they claim belongs to them, when it in fact falls within the area allotted to us by the Egyptian government. What is the evidence? The original deed, which is in our possession and which provides incontrovertible proof, is stored with dozens of other deeds, and work is currently underway to extract it; it is also said that there is an additional deed proving the Karaites’ ownership of the land. But since our brothers continue to be adamant about their claim to the boundary area, ignoring the existence of the deed, one of the members of the Basatin committee pointed out that the matter is simple and does not require recourse to proof or deeds, since it is well known that the Karaites observe a special regime in burying the dead, which is distinct to that of our brothers. Namely, it is our custom to dig graves vertically, and after reaching a depth of approximately two meters we make a lateral opening the same size as the grave, in which the body is buried, then this opening is stopped up with brick, and earth is thrown in. Our brothers, on the other hand, simply dig vertically—a form of burial known as the Tunisian fashion. Moreover, it is customary when a Karaite dies to bury them with their {{em:tallit}}, followed by the {{em:sisit}}, which is braided in our distinctive manner using only the colors white and blue, whereas that of our brothers is multicolored. Likewise, they attach no importance to burying a {{em:tallit}} with the deceased. It was therefore decided to exhume one of the bodies buried in the contested area of land between the two sections—for necessity knows no laws—and it was found that the burial method used matched that of the Karaites; furthermore, a {{em:tallit}} was found with braided threads in white and blue; and finally, it was also observed that the body was wearing underwear beneath the winding sheet, which is Karaite practice. In the face of all this evidence there can be no doubt that the land belongs to the Karaites, since it shows that our forefathers buried their dead there over the last century. Yet even placing this evidence to one side, the land still incontestably belongs to us by virtue of the law of adverse possession, a fact borne out by the grave that was opened. I do not know whether or not our brothers are persuaded by this mass of evidence that the land belongs to us; what I fear is that the matter may end up being decided in a court of law, which is something no Israelite can countenance—and in any case, the matter should not be allowed to cause strife at a time when maintaining harmonious and friendly relations is of crucial importance.

One hopes that after our differences have been amicably settled, work can begin on demarcating the land at Basatin, laying it out according to a formal plan, and increasing grants of land on the boundary area to members of the community in order to encourage them to bury their dead there, so that we can line the boundary with graves and enclosures and in so doing preserve ownership over the area for future generations.

What I would like to say to members of our community is that our graves are unfortunately a model of chaos and disorder. One glance over Basatin is enough to give you a very unfavourable impression of the graves, for some point north and others south, some are on raised ground while others are on low ground, there are more than a hundred graves crammed into one small area scarcely separated by half a metre while nearby lies a huge expanse abandoned to squawking crows, and there are enclosures on the eastern side and others on the western in no discernible order. Wherever you walk are heaps of sand, and if you should inadvertently step on or trip over one, you will suddenly find human bones scattered before you, or the skull of a child who was buried with only a handful of earth scattered over their body, and no thought given to a gravestone to mark their final resting-place; instead it is left to be stamped on by passers-by, who trample it beneath their feet and dislodge it with their shoes. Pity the poor child who tasted deprivation while living on this earth, where living beings were cruel, then found, in death, that the dead too were cruel, for they would not make space among them. This child was not fated to find rest in life or in death.

And meanwhile, visitor to al-Basatin, if you turn and cast your gaze behind you it will fall upon our brothers’ land, where you will good taste, geometry and order plainly manifested: the land is divided into plots, the graves form neat rows, trees have been planted, each family has their own plot, and every enclosure is built in the neatest and most felicitous fashion.
It is our sincere hope that the Basatin committee and its capable members embark on this undertaking, which is their responsibility, as soon and as conscientiously as possible.
Ili Amin Lishaʿ

paragraphs.english: The Karaite Jews used to hold their legal hearings in the home of their religious leader, that is to say the {{em:hakham akbar}}’s house, which was known as {{em:bayt al-din}} or {{em:dar al-sharʿ}}, meaning house of the law. Hearings would take place in the presence of the {{em:hakham akbar}} and community notables. The document reproduced on the cover of this issue by photo-zincography is, like the previous document, composed in Hebrew letters though the pronunciation is Arabic, and is in the possession of the esteemed Dr. Ibrahim Minashsha. Here we give the text of the document in Arabic letters. It is a section from a court case which was held 135 years ago according to the Hebrew calendar:

The occasion for the writing down of these letters as record of their occurrence is that the notables, God bless them, attended the house of the law, may its name be esteemed, in the home of the venerable {{em:hakham}} Mr. Abraham Levi, God preserve him and reward him well, son of the respected {{em:hakham}}Yaʿqub Levi, may God grant him dwellings in the gardens of Eden. They summoned Yusif ibn Yahuda Minashsha with his sister ʿAziza in relation to the case of the estate of their late paternal uncle Shalomo [sic] Minashsha, after they had already met ten times instead of one, with no understanding reached. The events had taken place and they called upon the aforementioned Yusif and his aforementioned sister ʿAziza to give testimony; the same Yusif appeared and donated to his sister, the same ʿAziza, four thousand {{em:nisf}} {{em:fadda}}, and next Shalomo ben Yashuʿa Minashsha appeared, and showed them good sense and gave five hundred {{em:nisf fadda}} of his own to his cousin ʿAziza on top of the four thousand which her brother Yusif had given her, by agreement and mutual consent amongst them all.

The {{em:hakham}} and notables sent for and questioned the same ʿAziza, with five trustworthy witnesses, and she said to them, “Yes, I have reached a satisfactory agreement with my brother and we have reconciled, and I am no longer owed anything by my brother from my uncle’s estate,” and declared in front of the five witnesses that she did not have any claim to any of her aforementioned late uncle Shalomo’s remaining effects, and nor did she have any form of dependence upon her brother Yusif, for better or worse,{{fn:12}} and no demand or request; no thread, copper, clay pot or oddment out of all the effects [of] the estate left by her uncle; the witnesses who had questioned her were witness to that, and then they returned. She signalled her approval with the entire response before the {{em:hakham}} and the notables, in the presence of the witnesses and those present whose signatures are below. Recorded on Sunday, eighth day of the month of Kislev in the year 5572 of creation, corresponding to the Arabic month of Qaʿda in the year 1226 of the {{em:hijri}} calendar and everything written here is faithful, true, fixed, and legally binding.

articles.title: The Neighborhood Synagogue is Closed—Open it up Again

paragraphs.english: The doors of the neighborhood synagogue, Dar Simhah, are closed due to the building’s dilapidated state. The congregation are no longer able to pray there. Residents of the neighborhood currently pray in a small room on the premises of the Karaite Jewish Schools in Egypt. This state of affairs cannot continue and members of the community will not tolerate having to conduct prayers outside of the synagogue for any length of time.
{{center:Let Us Act}}

We must join forces and work together to rebuild the synagogue now that the Communal Council has decided that it should be demolished and rebuilt entirely, in an extraordinary session attended by his excellency the {{em:Hakham Akbar}} Tubiyah Simhah Lifi Babufitsh. Amongst the conditions which the {{em:Hakham}} stipulated was that the new synagogue be funded by donations from members of the community.

This was in light of the fact that funds in the community’s coffers are reserved for major projects planned for the future and for assistance to the poor. A large number of community members approved of this idea and promised to fulfil the condition by gathering the funding necessary to rebuild the neighborhood synagogue Dar Simhah and hold prayers there, out of their personal contributions.

To the generous and munificent—offer your assistance and donate what you can, and may God keep you in His grace, for you will have contributed to the building of a synagogue in which pure hearts may observe the duty of prayer to God the all-powerful and sublime.
The Communal Council

paragraphs.english: [blank paragraph]{{fn:13}}
paragraphs.comments: [13] According to a contemporary interviewed by Joel Beinin, “[t]he editors left blank spaces in articles in several issues following the bombing to protest the government’s handling of the incident and the censorship.” Joel Beinin, {{em:The Dispersion of Egyptian Jewry: Culture, Politics, and the Formation of a Modern Diaspora}} (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1998), 68.

paragraphs.english: At 5.30 on the morning of June 20, an hour when all is usually quiet, when all movement has fallen still, when eyelids are overpowered by drowsiness and people, unable to stave off sleep, surrender to a deep slumber…

The sound of two terrible explosions was heard, the first in the neighborhood of our brothers the Rabbanites, followed a few moments later by the second, some 150 metres away in the Karaite neighborhood.
Was this a child’s bomb?

Further explosions were to have taken place in various parts of the wider Jewish quarter. A cart was found in Darb al-Nasr, in the Karaite neighborhood, and another in another part of the area, each carrying a box packed with explosives and accompanied by a timer. The police also found quantities of the highly explosive substance gelignite scattered in a number of alleyways, but by God’s kindness and protection they did not detonate.

Explosives experts who examined the materials confirmed that the substance found on the ground and in one of the carts were sticks of the highly dangerous gelignite, while the box found in the second cart contained sticks of Nobel’s dynamite, the most hazardous type of explosive.
[Picture caption: Destruction caused by the explosions, which ripped out doors and windows]

The electric detonator wire, coated with rubber such that it could have been carried without arousing suspicion, was declared by the experts to be one of the most dangerous they had encountered, and could have detonated from the heat of a human hand. All the explosives used were so potent they could seep through human skin and cause headaches upon bodily contact.
Gratitude and appreciation

There is little we can do but offer our gratitude and appreciation to the men of the Egyptian police force, fire brigade and ambulance service, who performed their duty with sincere and honorable magnanimity and kindness, and were sparks of activity, movement, initiative, courage, daring and chivalry. All went above and beyond the call of duty, and it is scarcely possible for us to impart to them the praise and esteem they are due.
No feud or enmity

One of the evening newspapers reported that there was a feud between Karaites and Rabbanites, and that hostility between the two groups was deeply rooted. These comments were attributed to a member of our community in the newspaper’s coverage. The young man in question, named ʿAdil Amin, telephoned us to inform us that the comments did not come from him, and stressed that there was nothing but harmony and affection between us and our brothers.
[blank paragraph].
The Editor [Yusif Kamal]

paragraphs.english: {{center:The Blessed Month of Ramadan}}

The blessed month of Ramadan begins on Thursday July 8th 1948, and we offer warm wishes to our Muslim brothers on the commencement of this holy month. May God bring the country many returns of prosperity, goodness and blessing.
{{center:Extraordinary Session}}

The Communal Council convened an extraordinary Session last Saturday June 26th to discuss the situation of victims of the explosions in the neighborhood, as well as meeting in ordinary session on Tuesday June 29th for the same purpose.
{{center:Criminal Act}}

Speaking to a reporter from the newspaper {{em:Akhbar al-Yawm}}, his excellency the Grand Rabbi Hayyim Nahum Effendi condemned the explosion which took place in the Jewish quarter, calling it an intolerable criminal act. He added that he would have expressed his opinions on the matter fully and frankly were it not for the public prosecutor’s investigation, which is still ongoing. Responsibility for the attack has not yet been determined.
The Grand Rabbi concluded, “A criminal group which sees fit to cause the loss of human life cannot be tolerated under any circumstances.”
{{center:Special Fast}}

The first Thursday after the dreadful attack which took place in the neighborhood was a day of fasting and prayer, in which those affected refrained from eating and drinking, and were joined by other members of the community in gratitude to God the all-powerful and sublime for embracing them in His mercy and absolution.
{{center:Donations In Kind}}

Donations by the charitable to victims of the blasts in the neighborhood included bread, cheese, olives, eggs, dried fish, quantities of watermelon and cantaloupe, clothes, pyjamas, shirts, and soap. We kindly ask donors to telephone the Dar al-Sharʿ for information on victims’ needs before making donations in kind, as duplication has made certain donations redundant.
{{center:Kosher Meats}}

In recent days, many households have refrained from purchasing meat at kosher-licensed butchers over concerns that the animals are not being slaughtered according to kosher standards. We urge those in charge to look into the matter and issue a statement which will put an end to these doubts.
{{center:Congratulations}}

In a joyful family gathering last Thursday June 20th, the engagement was announced of our colleague the story-writer and social commentator Fuʾad Dabbah to Miss Nelly Barukh al-ʿAssal. We congratulate the couple and wish them all our best.

articles.title: A New Stage in the Community’s Life

paragraphs.english: February 14th last will go down as a momentous day that the community will remember forever, for on this date a contract of purchase was signed for the new community building, which thereby entered into our ownership. The building is located in one of Cairo’s loveliest neighbourhoods, at number 7 Sirgani Street in eastern ʿAbbasiyyah where peace and quiet reign; it is composed of three floors measuring 1560 meters, and additional buildings come to 320 meters, which is enough to meet all of the community’s needs.

We are delighted to take this opportunity to offer our good wishes: we congratulate the esteemed communal council on their successful conclusion of this deal, thanks to which the community may now proudly count the building amongst its properties, and we likewise congratulate the various individuals and groups who have long made the case for establishing an institution that would function as a centre around which their hearts and endeavors might rally. We would like to offer personal congratulations to the lawyer Murad Farag who has worked towards this goal for many years, and in doing so has been unstinting with both his time and money. Were it not for a sense of propriety, we would also mention here the efforts of {{em:al-Kalim}} and its longstanding campaign, which has finally met with success.

At a time of such effusive joy we would like to keep in mind various facts and figures, and the significant duties they entail. Upon signing the final contract we paid the remaining instalment of the cost, which amounted to 10,000 LE, having already paid 1,700 LE upon signing the initial contract. The total cost, including fees, came to approximately 12,120 LE. The community’s funds were not sufficient to cover the full amount, so the esteemed members of the communal council contributed various sums, as did a number of private individuals, who contributed approximately 1,000 LE so that we could afford the full cost. It is worthy of both note and gratitude that his excellency the {{em:Hakham Akbar}}kindly attended the session of the communal council in which the conclusion of the purchase was discussed, and donated a large sum of money, which persuaded members of the necessity of doing likewise—and indeed not one person declined to contribute.

In light of this information, it should be plainly clear that the community’s finances now stand at zero, or rather, below zero. The communal council was obliged to use community funds out of lack of time and a desire to conclude the purchase by any means possible and as fast as possible. There is work required now to restore the community to good financial health; we should consider the sums expended from community funds as debts hanging around our neck, which must be repaid in order to bring matters back into balance and allow the funds of the endowment [{{em:waqf}}] to be paid into to the endowment.

It is not only the repayment of these loans which is incumbent upon us. It should be obvious that in order to make the building ready to host community activities, some refurbishment and redecoration will be required, in addition to the purchase of furniture for its many rooms, which will cost no insignificant amount of money.

Alongside the financial requirements, there are a number of other obstacles to be overcome, including the fact that there is currently no available space in the building, all three floors of which are inhabited by tenants. The communal council must therefore seek to evacuate the building by legal and amicable means, since the building can offer no benefit to us in the present circumstances except for the income it provides in rent.

The first steps that need to be taken include moving the school to the new premises by the start of the coming school year; moving the {{em:hakhamkhanah}} and its administrative functions, along with the various community associations and clubs; preparing an office and a lecture hall and furnishing a room for marriage ceremonies; and so on.

This is only a small selection of the many things we have to consider. The important thing is that we do not rush headlong into the task, making things up as we go along. The communal council must proceed according to an established policy, and must put in place a carefully considered plan with a fixed timescale so that we may achieve our aims, and the good results we hope they will produce, on a solid and unshakeable basis. May God guide our steps and endow us with sense and integrity.
Yusif Kamal

articles.cover_caption: On the cover: “A happy new year and a new era. View of the {{em:haykal}} of Rabbi Simhah synagogue, showing the candelabras lit on the eve of the new year holiday”
articles.title: Give Us Back Our Dignity

paragraphs.english: Weeks have passed, and month has followed month, and again and again I hear of, and sometimes witness for myself, a peculiar scene repeating itself. A tragedy which concludes by trampling a woman’s dignity and demeaning her, leaving a stain of shame on the brow of the community. Has our young men’s virtue been totally obliterated? Do our young men not have a heart which beats for anything other than money? Or eyes which behold but the beauty of tinkling gold? Have they cast aside all morals, wisdom and maturity, made money their king and prostrated themselves before it? If that is so then you must admit that the community is done for.

The reason for the disgraceful backwardness which has dogged the community throughout the stages of its life is the dismal attitude of some of our young men, which leads to the spread of ignorance and illiteracy amongst members of the community in a most lamentable manner.

Any mature person who is educated, refined and possessed of good morals must be able to recognise that a woman is demeaned if a man abandons her for the sake of a few pounds. Our young men today, as far as I can see, do not care who will be their life partner or soul mate; all they care about is finding a playmate for their pocket-book. How many young women have felt that stab in the heart, had their hopes crushed, because of their inability to satisfy a “respectable” suitor with a dowry that is to his liking?

A father is obliged to prepare, from the moment his daughter is born, for the battle he will have to wage when she reaches marriageable age. Denying his own needs, living frugally, and exhausting himself in all manner of employment, he saves what he can as if arming himself for that battle.

And when the young woman grows up and is ready for marriage, the suitor arrives with that charming question on his lips: how much have you got? He is told the sum, and replies that it is paltry and insufficient; turning his back on her, he goes off in search of another young lady who will give him what he covets.

I consider our young men too good to stoop to this pitiful level, and it saddens me to think that we young women of the community are mere commodities to be bought and sold. We command no respect or esteem in the eyes of young men. Young men, give us back our dignity and save us from this malady which has struck you in the heart and blinded your vision, turning us into your victims. Educated young men, in one hand you hold our happiness and delight, and in the other our wretchedness and misery, so listen to the voice of your conscience, if indeed you have a living conscience. Know that if we have tolerated this ignominy today, tomorrow we shall not.

This does not mean I am inciting the girls of my sex to revolution against you; rather, I am calling upon them to demand the rights which have been denied them, and the status of which they have been robbed, so that we may keep pace with this age of equality, progress and advancement.

articles.title: {{em:Mughat}}

paragraphs.english: {{em:Mughat}}{{fn:14}} comes to Egypt from Iraq and is sold in markets in the form of woody roots of different shapes and sizes. The plant is native to the north of Iraq and the regions on the Iranian border, on neglected rocky foothills. The name {{em:mughat}} is used only by Egyptians and the Baghdadi traders who export it to Egypt; in Iraq it is more commonly known as {{em:ʿarab qawzi}}, meaning ‘Arab nut’ in the language of the Turkmen people who live in the regions where it grows—a name which it acquired because some Iraqis eat its seeds like chickpeas. In Iran it is called {{em:denderu}}.

However, it is almost only Egyptians, and natives of other Eastern countries who have spent time among them, who prepare {{em:mughat}}. The {{em:mughat}} trade is dominated by Iraqis, while the plant is gathered by villagers in the regions where it grows. After gathering, it is dried in the open air for several days then packed in sacks and transported to Egypt. Cultivation in Egypt was attempted for the first time in 1932, and it was found that the Egyptian variety produced a pleasant-tasting drink.

It is not known precisely when {{em:mughat}} was first imported from Iraq to Egypt, though it was probably during the Abbasid period when the two countries enjoyed close ties. {{em:Mughat}} was a source of confusion to Arab doctors, as well as the European doctors who learned from them, and is mentioned in many Arabic literary works. However, it appears those who wrote about it had only seen its roots or seeds. Such was the case with Ibn al-Baytar, who was punctilious in describing plants that he had seen and therefore did not give a description of {{em:mughat}}, which he had not. Ibn Sina [Avicenna] wrote that it “strengthens the limbs; is fattening, efficacious in the treatment of breakage and contusion, and efficacious for gout, convulsions, and joint stiffness; and alleviates stiffness in the throat and lungs.” Dawud al-Antaki observed that it grew in al-Karkh, adjacent to Baghdad, and its islands and mountains, and that its roots are tough and grow deep into the ground, with a black-red exterior which peels away to uncover a white-yellow flesh. The best kind is heavy, fragrant, and reddish in colour, with a slight bitterness. We know no more than this, but I have been told it has large, rough leaves like radish leaves, white flowers, and seeds very similar to {{em:habb al-simnah}} which are known as {{em:qilqil}}. The pharmacologist ʾAzar Armaniyus wrote the following in 1922: “Wild pomegranate is the name the Arabs give to {{em:qilqil}}, the roots of which are known commercially as {{em:mughat}}. It comes from the land of the Arabs and is used in Egypt as a medicinal powder, which is mixed with sugar, infused in milk, or boiled in water. It is used to invigorate and strengthen patients weakened by chronic chest or venereal illnesses, and to help new mothers recover their strength. {{em:Mughat}} is prepared in Egypt as a fortifying drink, which is given to women for seven days after childbirth, and is consumed more generally for strength, nutrition, and warmth in winter. {{em:Mughat}} is ground into a fine, yellowish-white powder which can be used alone—called “plain {{em:mughat}}”—and prepared as a drink by browning the {{em:mughat}} in ghee then boiling it in water with a large quantity of sugar. Alternatively, it can be mixed with other ingredients, a preparation known as “spiced {{em:mughat}}”. {{em:Mughat}} is rich in gluten and carbohydrates but low in protein, and contains only traces of fat, which is why ghee and protein-rich ground seeds are added to make it a highly nutritional drink.

articles.title: Diaries of an Apprentice in the Goldsmithing Quarter

paragraphs.english: {{em:May 26}}

Today {{em:khawagah}}{{fn:15}} Lyitu hit me with his cane, hard, because I had mistakenly—so he claimed—put gas in the crucible instead of acid, even though I hadn’t been anywhere near the crucible all day… But I was too scared to say so. I was too scared to tell him that it was he himself who had prepared the crucible, before sending me an hour ago to {{em:khawagah}}Shabtay’s shop to borrow a wooden mallet. I was too scared to tell him any of that, or else he might hit me and hurt me even more.
paragraphs.comments: [15] A title of respect used when addressing non-Muslims, which has subsequently come to mean ‘foreigner’.

paragraphs.english: {{em:June 16}}

The boss sent me to fetch his lunch from his house as usual, and there I saw his younger daughter Suzette riding back and forth on the back of a colorful wooden rocking-horse. I remembered the swing bed and I suddenly felt an urge to jump astride the horse, if only for a moment… I gazed at Suzette with imploring eyes, and as if she understood the meaning of my look she dismounted from her rocking-horse and waved to me to climb on.
Fearfully and vigilantly, she hopped about, checking whether her mother was watching or was still cooking in the kitchen.

I was reassured, but no sooner had I placed one foot ready to climb astride than the lady appeared. Seeing me, what did she do but give me a smack around the face so hard it felt like my head had come off my body. I was aware of the lady screaming at me, threatening to complain to the {{em:khawagah}} if I ever so much as came near her daughter again, or touched any of her toys. I burst into tears out of pain and frustration. I promised her I would never do it again.
{{em:June 17}}

I tried to sleep last night, but oh!—the image of the rocking-horse refused to leave my mind, and I tossed and turned as if on hot coals of wishing and wanting, thinking over and over about how Suzette’s mother had hit me so hard, and for no reason… The tears only poured down my cheeks harder, and my heart only burnt more fiercely, as I sighed to myself, “What have I done to deserve this torture, Lord?”
If only my mother would buy me a rocking-horse!
{{em:July 6}}

Suzette hasn’t tried to talk to me since the day her mother hit me, and whenever she sees me she runs away so that I won’t see her. I don’t know whether she’s scared of me or feels sorry for me, worrying that if I see her I might remember how her mother humiliated me. I glimpsed her vanishing yesterday and it seemed to me that there was a look of sympathy and pain in her eyes. How I hate it that that little girl should pity me. And how I wish her rocking-horse would shatter into pieces, that horse that earned me a smack out of no fault of my own.
If only my father would buy me a rocking-horse!
{{em:July 9}}

Something strange happened today. I saw {{em:khawagah}} Lyitu crying in the workshop, then laughing, and staggering and talking strangely; then he started to sing in his gruff voice, “Oh beautiful Edirne, they’ve occupied you…”

Hearing the racket, {{em:khawagah}} Yusif from next door appeared. When he saw the state the boss was in, he grasped him by the hand and said: “Uncle Lyitu, this isn’t on. It hardly looks respectable. Really, my man, do you have to get drunk in the shop? Come on now, get up and we’ll go home.” With that he led him away by the hand and took him back to his house, and told me to shut up shop and go home.

It was only late afternoon and I was worried my mother would ask me why I was home early. In my mind, I went over what {{em:khawagah}} Yusif had said: “Really, my man, do you have to get drunk in the shop?” {{em:Sakran}}… Drunk. Where had I heard that word before? Yes, that was it—last Saturday, as we were leaving Cinema Ramses. On the way home, I had seen a man staggering along, holding a stick in one hand, which he brandished threateningly at a group of children who had surrounded him and were shouting an insulting rhyme: “{{em:Sakran tinah, harami al-katinah}}!”{{fn:16}}
paragraphs.comments: [16] The rhyme calls the man a drunk and a thief.

paragraphs.english: I remembered now something which I had missed before. {{em:Khawagah}} Lyitu, when he claimed I had put gas in the crucible instead of acid and hit me, had been swaying slightly in his walk, and singing “Oh beautiful Edirne…” Yes, I saw it now. He had been drunk!
I meandered through the streets, wondering why it was that {{em:khawagah}} Lyitu got drunk. I arrived home after lingering a little longer than usual in the streets and alleys.
{{em:August 3}}

Yesterday I went past the neighborhood school, where groups of pupils were playing outside. How splendid they looked in their beautiful uniforms, each with a red tarboush perched smartly on their head and a bag of books and pens and pencils in hand.

As I was admiring the schoolchildren going back and forth—one of them reading a book, and another a newspaper, while others were deep in conversation—I spotted our neighbors’ son, Salih (or Salih Effendi as he was known, since in our neighborhood people were used to calling anyone wearing a suit and tarboush “effendi”) so I raised a hand in greeting.

To my great dismay, Salih took one look at my sooty black clothes and hands and moved away, ignoring me as if we were not neighbours. It pierced my heart, but I quickly saw the reason for his aversion to me: those pupils—those effendis—wore clean, neat clothes, while I only had a torn and faded robe, which barely kept the winter cold or the searing summer dust at bay. It was true, those effendis and I could not be more different. If only I were an effendi too, then I could go to school, and Salih Effendi would respect me!
{{em:August 12}}

Tonight I came home exhausted, my nerves in pieces; I could scarcely close my eyes without a shudder running through my limbs. It had been a terrifying, eventful night. On my way home, I turned down Khan Abu Taqiyyah Street, as usual, just as nightfall was spreading its black wings. The dim lights of the gas lamps hanging over the houses danced in the darkness, casting vague shadows onto the road that seemed to make the silence even deeper and more dreadful. As I hurried down that desolate street, the silence was pierced by a terrifying cackle that sounded more like a demon than a human being. It reverberated back and forth in the deserted street, the blank walls of the houses returning its echo. I glanced around in fright, and to my horror, there behind me at the corner of the street was a colossal giant, whose head nearly reached the balconies of the houses around him. He was blacker than the deepest night. Sparks flew from his eyes as if from flaming arrows. In his hand he carried a stick, and was using it to smash the lanterns above the houses, one by one. Each time one shattered, he leapt into the air and gave a cackle so loud it seemed the very sky would break open.

My heart practically jumping out of my chest, I stood stock-still. Sweat poured down my brow. I tried to scream but the sound died on my lips, as if a hand were gripping my throat to stop me making any noise. I tried to run, but my feet were nailed to the ground.

The darkness got thicker every time that terrifying devil shattered another lantern, and the street was quickly plunged into coal-black darkness. Gone were the sparks shooting from the demonic eyes, as if they were not strong enough to resist the heavy, engulfing darkness and instead had chosen to withdraw. It seemed to me that a searing wind had drawn him down into the belly of the earth, or perhaps upward into the sky. The street was silent again. I slowly began to feel my way through the deep darkness until I reached the house, where I surrendered my body to my bed and my soul to tears.
I certainly would not walk home that way again. I didn’t want to be caught unawares by {{em:ʿafarit}}!{{fn:17}}
(to be continued…)
Muris Farid Musa

articles.title: Passover {{em:Fitir}}{{fn:18}}

paragraphs.english: The matter of Passover {{em:fitir}} is an annual theme that recurs, as surely as the days go by and the heavens turn, every time the blessed holiday of Passover comes around. The surprising thing is that despite many years’ experience making {{em:fitir}}, and despite the many crises that have occurred in relation to {{em:fitir}} production, our community is still getting to grips with the process. Every year the same complaints arise as in previous years. In order to understand these complaints, let us examine them here one by one.
1. {{em:Wheat, milling, and flour:}}

The most important factor in the process is the purchase of a clean, high-grade quality of wheat which will produce white flour. We have customarily found Indian golden wheat, which the community purchases from the Royal Agricultural Society out of leftover sowing grain, suitable for this purpose.

I have no objection to this practice, but the price must be lower than the selling price of the grain, which is approximately 800 piasters more than the ordinary price per {{em:ardabb}}[of grain sold for consumption], since the community is not going to use it for sowing (because the distribution season ends [before Passover], what the community buys comes from the leftovers of grain used for sowing).

This year, I suggest that we purchase imported Australian wheat, which is a very clean variety of wheat, sold at 3.300 LE per {{em:ardabb,}} available from the granaries of Banque Misr and the Credit Bank. It produces a bright white flour of a firm quality that is perfectly suited to making {{em:fitir}}.

Milling, meanwhile, is of crucial importance, with two factors to consider: first, the mill must be large enough that the wheat purchased does not mix with whatever was milled there immediately beforehand, and can be milled in a single batch; second, the community must be prepared to sacrifice two or three {{em:ardabb}}s of wheat in order to clean out the mill before milling.
2. {{em:Preparation of the oven:}}

As is well known, rats and mice often feed and make their homes in ovens; as is also well known, mice are impure, especially when dead. Therefore, all cracks and gaps in the oven should be stopped up during repainting so that no mice come into contact with whatever is being baked. It is also advisable to have the oven cleaned so as to remove any traces that harmful vermin or insects may have left behind.

The {{em:fitir-}}makers themselves are dirty by nature, and this must be mitigated by forcing them to bathe thrice weekly. Each should be bought two sets of clothes, one for work and one for sleep; sleep clothes should not be used for work and vice versa.

I remember I once took exception to the filthy state of a {{em:fitir}}-maker and he complained to me that there was no soap. Therefore, soap should be provided so that want of it cannot be used as an excuse for the workers’ dirtiness.
Workers by nature take surveillance and oversight of their work into account, and as the level of surveillance and oversight increases, so too does the workers’ precision and productivity.
3. {{em:Producing}} fitir{{em::}}

Making {{em:fitir}} is subject to a certain degree of improvisation, and it is therefore advisable that a rough count of members of the community be compiled, starting now, with each person stating the quantity of {{em:fitir}} they require, so an estimate can be made of the quantity required in each pack. This would have the benefit of eliminating corruption of the type where a “customer” goes to the bakery and slips the baker a tip, in return for which the baker selects the best {{em:fitir}} for the customer—when really all {{em:fitir}} should be of the best kind possible. Any tips could instead be collected and distributed between all the workers at the end of the season.

I also believe that customers should be prohibited absolutely from entering the bakery from the very beginning of the distribution season, and that orders made on behalf of others should also be absolutely prohibited, for all members of the community alike.
I shall return to the topic of flour and price at a later date.
Farag Yaʿqub Aslan

paragraphs.english: It gives us great pleasure to publish here a letter sent to the communal council, accompanying a generous donation, by the esteemed Musa Murad, a member of that council. Mr Murad’s aim in making this donation was to honor the memory of his beloved grandfather the late Musa Murad, known as Murdukh, who is remembered for his strong faith, gentle disposition, kind heart, placid manner, generosity and noble-mindedness. The letter needs no comment. May it embolden other charity-givers to come forward and emulate his virtuous example; and may God reward them with a generosity ten times their own in this life and the next.
—The Editor
To the esteemed President of the Communal Council of the Karaite Jews in Egypt,
I wish to present the donation outlined below to the first session of the higher council, for which I thank you in advance.

God has blessed me and my home so generously that I prostrate myself in gratitude for the happiness I enjoy. With His assistance—may He be exalted—I hereby undertake to personally finance construction of the upper floor of the {{em:Hakhamkhanah}}, next to the Dar Simhah synagogue at 50 Khurunfish St, to house a charitable clinic for the poor of our beloved community, so the pain of those suffering may be relieved as God relieved the pains of my children, in particular my daughter Liyuni whom He cured and whose life He saved.

So that the clinic will be able to continue its work, I hereby donate my share, amounting to five {{em:qirat}} and sixteen {{em:sahm}} (approximately 992 square meters), in the property located at no. 10, Suq al-Sayarif al-Saghir (the small money-changers’ market), known as al-Sagha al-Gadida (the new goldsmithing quarter), in al-Gamaliyyah, Cairo; enclosed herewith is the contract, in order for you to undertake the measures necessary to effect this donation. Likewise enclosed is the sum of twenty-five Egyptian pounds and five hundred millimes, equal to the same share of the total rent for the months January to March 1950. Also enclosed are four bonds, year 911 [1911?], of the Egyptian Land Bank, numbers 143361, 43732, 133949, 162711, and their coupons numbers 39-50, so that if God wills—may He be glorified and exalted—and they are profitable, the returns may be used to expand the clinic so that it can treat all types of illnesses. In conclusion, I ask that God grant all of us the strength to serve our beloved community.
Please accept my sincerest respects.
God’s humble servant,
Musa Murad Musa

articles.title: What kind of {{em:Fitir}} is this…!{{fn:19}}

paragraphs.english: If this year’s {{em:fitir}} had a virtue, it was justice. Yes, justice—and what justice indeed.

There weren’t two grades of {{em:fitir}} this year. There wasn’t one kind of well-made, appetising {{em:fitir}}, and another that was poor quality and unappealing; instead, all the {{em:fitir}} was of the latter kind.

A respected member of the Communal Council wrote an article on the subject of {{em:fitir}} in {{em:al-Kalim}} last January that was full of promises and assurances. Nothing has come of them save the promise to end nepotism, and indeed this year there wasn’t one kind for some and a better kind for others; rather, this year’s {{em:fitir}} were all the same kind, which was distributed to everyone without exception.
And so, everybody was treated unjustly—but injustice, if meted out fairly, is justice!

The {{em:fitir}} had another virtue, but one which hid a painful truth within it—“good on the outside, bad on the inside”, as the saying goes—and that was its wrapping. The {{em:fitir}} were wrapped in paper, each paper package ostensibly containing ten{{em:fitir}}. Yet nobody opening the wrapping could count ten{{em:fitir}} because it in fact contained hundreds of broken pieces of {{em:fitir}}that were impossible to count. Seldom did one come across a piece the size of half or even a quarter of a {{em:fitir}}, only oddly-shaped fragments; and yet they were all the same thickness, so you couldn’t tell if they came from the centre or the edge of the {{em:fitir}}. Every paper package seemed to contain only hard, bony, lumpy edge pieces akin to fragments of stone.
If only that were all—but the pieces were splotched black with soot from the oven, and some were burnt while others were uncooked.

And thus this year’s {{em:fitir}} were so poorly made that complaints abounded. It grieves us to say that we are obliged to print yet another article on this topic every year, to the point that we’re sick and tired of writing them and our dear readers are too.

“No believer falls into the same trap twice,”{{fn:21}} yet we fall into the same trap every year. Must we learn nothing from the mistakes of the past? And is making {{em:fitir}}really so difficult that each year’s {{em:fitir}} must turn out worse than the last’s?
Where is the {{em:fitir}} committee?
Where is the committee, which has now been convening and concluding, discussing and deliberating, resolving and enacting, for over four months?

Where is the committee, which counts among its members individuals famous for their energy and productivity, and for their strenuous opposition to, stinging criticism of, and technical advice concerning the {{em:fitir}}-making process of previous years—before they themselves joined the ranks of those responsible?
What has the committee achieved?
First we were given bony, crumbling, soot-smeared bits of dough that they called {{em:fitir}}.
Then what? The price went up!
Then what? The number of broken pieces added insult to injury.

I wanted to headline my article “What is this sooty mess?,” but I asked God’s pardon for presuming to describe a blessing in such a way, even if it is the sad truth. So I tactfully entitled the article, “What kind of {{em:fitir}} is this?” I hope the headline of next year’s article will be “Now that’s what I call {{em:fitir}}.”
Yusif Kamal
