articles.title: Those who can, Pay your Tithes

paragraphs.english: One thing reminds one of another. I was prompted to write this article by what happened in the Great Synagogue on the Feast of Atonement [{{em:ʿId al-Istighfar}}], since what happened was because of a request for tithes.

The {{em:hakham akbar}} has called for the payment and delivery of tithes since his arrival in Egypt, in fulfilment of the commandments of the Torah. Many people share his belief yet only a few have actually delivered their tithes—so few they can be counted on two hands. Why do so few people who believe in tithing actually pay? I will explain the reason here.

While I was with the Kohanim at the ark [{{em:ekhal}}] on the Day of Atonement, the esteemed {{em:hakham}} said to one of the Kohanim who was of sufficient means, “Mr So-and-so, you ought to pay your tithes.” The response was “God willing.” This response signifies consent to deliver, and that should be done as soon as possible.

On the same day, the {{em:hakham}} asked a distinguished member of the community to help him lead the main prayer, and the person in question was next to him during the prayers. When he knelt in prostration, the {{em:hakham}} said, “Mr So-and-so, pay your tithes,” and when he stood up again, he said “Mr So-and-so, pay your tithes,” to the point it was said he had asked the person in question to deliver his tithes twenty times on the feast day alone.

The esteemed {{em:hakham}} has his own method of making requests, which is to do so without a codified policy. I have met with many members of the community and found that they are perfectly willing to deliver their tithes, but—that’s right, there is a but—they politely make their excuses, not because they are too poor, but because the rich of the community have not paid theirs.

So if the esteemed {{em:hakham}} wishes to guarantee the delivery of tithes within a year or even six months or less, he should unify his efforts and direct them towards seven of the community’s richest members—and if those seven pay up then I will personally guarantee the rest.

Restrict your efforts, esteemed {{em:hakham}}, to the very wealthy first of all, for if you persuade them then the matter is solved. It isn’t right that the poor should pay before the well-off, the well-off before the rich, and the rich before the extremely rich: the richest must pay first.
There are around seven people whom the esteemed {{em:hakham}} knows well, some of whom are amongst his close and faithful friends, so why do they not fulfil his request?
Those who wish to pay do not need persuading, and nor do they need time; most of what is requested is determined by seriousness and persuasiveness of the person requesting.
Murad Farag

paragraphs.english: {{center:To all members of the Karaite community in Cairo}}
Dear brothers,

Further to my previous correspondence with you, it gives me great pleasure to add the following. It will be no secret to you that our religion is presently in a more parlous state of decline than has ever before been the case. There is no doubt that if we do not take certain measures, then our community might conceivably disappear entirely from the earth. Yet there is no level of difficulty that cannot be overcome as long as there is courage and firm resolve to do so, and the first step is to analyse the present situation and the measures necessary to ameliorate it. Given the difficulty it would present me to visit you I propose that a number of you, both men of religion and secular, come to Paris to meet with me; I think it preferable that such a meeting take place before summer this year. If you accept this proposal then I ask you to do me the honour of informing me to this effect, and of informing me which date you think best for our meeting in Paris, several weeks in advance so that the necessary arrangements may be made for it to take place.

I believe that our religious community suffers from an unfortunate lack of men of religion and scholars who are well-versed in our teachings, and thus I believe it would be wise to consider sending a number of your young men to pursue specialized studies in religion in Paris, which is home to many scholars of international repute. Even if those young men do not devote their later lives to religion, their education will not be in vain, but will always be of use to them.

There are also a great number of weighty matters to examine and discuss during our meeting in Paris, and I am always most willing to correspond with any of you who wish to acquaint yourselves with these matters or discuss them with me. You may write to me in any language you see fit.
I ask you to do me the great honor of publishing this letter in your esteemed organ {{em:al-Kalim}}.
Please accept the sincerest gratitude of your faithful servant,
Simon Szyszman
61, rue Brancion, Paris 15e, France

articles.cover_caption: On the cover: “Community schools in the balance. Do the benefits outweigh the disadvantages??”
articles.title: The School Must Stay

paragraphs.english: The Karaite community in Egypt only has one institution of which it can be proud: the Karaite Jewish School, a venerable institution which was one of the first schools to be founded in Egypt and is now more than half a century old.

If we recall the history of this school—with its many achievements in educating the community, and the good things it has done for the many individuals who studied there and went on to become doctors, engineers, lawyers, traders and employees—it becomes clear that it has undertaken a noble and significant mission in education and edification for a substantial period of time.

It is therefore difficult for the community to contemplate its only institution being condemned to death. The school’s glorious history makes a convincing case for it to remain for many days and years to come.
We must weigh the school’s virtues alongside its shortcomings in order for public opinion to rule for or against it and decide whether it should stay or go.
{{em:Let us start with its virtues:}}
1. Symbolic and moral merit as the community’s sole institution.
2. Its glorious past and its many achievements in educating members of the community.
3. The excellent standard of the school’s teaching staff, most of whom are members of the community.
4. The dazzling primary certificate results obtained: in many years the school has achieved a 100% success rate.
5. The attention given to teaching Hebrew language and religion.
{{em:Now for the shortcomings:}}
1. The {{em:Dar al-Sharʾ}} loses approximately 1200 LE per year, of which 600 LE covers the rent of the school building at 50 LE per month.
2. The number of students at the school is 250, of which only 25 come from the community.
3. The school’s location in al-Khurunfish is one reason why it attracts low enrolment rates from the community.
4. The reduction in lottery income from 20 LE to 6 LE per month, which is deducted from the assistance disbursed by the Ministry of Education, amounting to 55 LE per semester.

5. {{em:Dar al-Sharʾ}} spends sums in the range of 200-250 LE per year on education, in addition to what it loses on the school. These sums represent the cost of children from the community attending the schools of our brothers and other secondary and higher schools, as well as the costs of an educational delegation in France.
6. The school has not become a middle school as laid out in the new policy but has remained an ordinary primary school.

These are some of the most significant virtues and shortcomings of the school. We hope the Communal Council will not be hasty in deciding one way or the other. Public opinion leans towards overcoming the problems, for example by starting work as soon as possible on moving the school to ʿAbbasiyyah so it can open in the coming academic year. A suitable premises could be found by advertising in newspapers, engaging agents, and so on, and the Ministry of Education would cover the rent of the new building while the {{em:Dar al-Sharʾ}} could make use of rent income from the current building; the new location would also encourage community members to enrol. Work could also begin on expanding the school into a middle school, and so on.

The community awaits with hand on heart the communal council’s decision, at its coming session, on the fate of the school. Public opinion wishes to overcome the challenges in retaining the school, which is the community’s only institution.
Abu Yaʿqub

articles.cover_caption: On the cover: “The Young Men’s Love of Torah Association celebrates Monsieur Simon Szyszman. The esteemed guest is shown at the left, and next to him Mr. Dafid Lishaʿ, {{em:gabbay}} of the synagogue, and next Mr. Jak Mangubi, president of the Communal Council”
articles.title: A Glimpse of the Karaite World

paragraphs.english: On the evening of Friday October 16th 1953, the famed scholar and writer Simon Szyszman, a member of the community in France, arrived in Cairo for the first time.
He was warmly received by the Karaite Jews’ {{em:Hakham Akbar}} Tubiyah Lifi Babufitsh, and a number of important men and young people from the community.

Simon is of Polish origin, and has always lived to serve the Karaites across Europe, where he proudly bears the flag of his religion. The writer has travelled in Poland, France, Russia and Turkey, where he has lectured on Karaite history for scholars, orientalists and history enthusiasts. He knows several languages, including Polish, Latin, Turkish, and Russian, which encourages him further in the proud accomplishment of his mission. He has published an article in {{em:al-Kalim}} on the origins of the Karaites.

I became acquainted with Monsieur Szyszman and corresponded with him in Paris, and when he visited Egypt I welcomed him warmly and met with him for a conversation. Being a keen amateur of Karaite history throughout the world I was proud to meet with him.

He told me that the largest Karaite Jewish community in existence before the outbreak of war in 1914 was in Russia. It numbered approximately 15,000 people, many of whom were prosperous, and counted philosophers, military leaders, writers and inventors among its number.

Among the military figures was a man famed for his courage, brilliance and intelligence named Mark Tapsashar, who won a decisive victory against the Japanese in 1904-5, teaching them a lesson in bravery and flair. When this hero died during a fierce battle, the Japanese army gave his body a military salute and recounted stories of his bravery to the Japanese emperor, even though he was their bitter enemy. His sword is preserved to this day in a museum in Tokyo.

Another notable Karaite was a man named Solomon Krym, a member of the Russian parliament who stood up for the rights of Karaites and Islam. Similarly, the learned philosopher Ilya Kazaz (died 1912) established a school of Islam in Russia and embodied both Eastern and Western cultures. There were many virtuous men besides these who earned the Karaites great repute.

When war broke out in 1914, he participated in it. Many Karaites were conscripted and many killed in the bloody conflict which ensued. When revolution erupted in 1917, the Karaites opposed the communist aggression and many young Karaites died as a result. When the communists came to power, they imprisoned many Karaites and executed a not inconsiderable number, while others died of hunger and poverty and synagogues were destroyed. The community was left with nothing and dwindled to 4,000 individuals.

At the end of the war in 1918 the Karaites found sympathy and esteem in Poland and Lithuania, where schools, synagogues and hospitals were built for them and financial help was given. Their situation improved greatly, writers and scholars emerged, there were three newspapers in existence and many books were published.

War broke out again from 1939-45 and Russia occupied Poland and the Lithuanian peninsula. Karaite synagogues and temples were turned into cinemas and private clubs, and Karaite populations began to slowly disappear.

When I asked about the number of Karaites in Paris, Szyszyman replied that there remain no more than two hundred elderly Karaites who are not organised and do not have a synagogue, and that the community will doubtless disappear within a matter of years. There is also a community of approximately 200 Karaites in Istanbul which will also vanish with the passing of time.

Szyszman then told me: “I came to Egypt to ask members of the Karaite Jewish community in Egypt to join forces and organise their efforts, and to realise that we have no Karaites other than our community in Egypt. They should show pride in their past and thereby raise our morale, for they are the pride of the past and the hope of the future.”

“I also see cause for pride in this new age of freedom, and in the men of the revolution, led by Commander-in-Chief Muhammad Nagib. I have heard much about him, his interest in our community, and his visit to our temple. May God grant him victory. I ask God, may He be glorified and exalted, to grant our community long life and urge its young people to work hand-in-hand for its best interests.”

Monsieur Szyszman concluded by saying, “I extend a warm greeting and a hand of brotherhood to all of the Karaites of Egypt, and hope that they take pride in our ancestors, so that our community will never dwindle or disappear. God is the guarantor of all success.”
Muris Tawil
College of Pharmacy, Strasbourg, France

articles.title: The Heliopolis Synagogue

paragraphs.english: Thanks to God’s mercy on this well-protected country, the sombre black clouds which once darkened its skies have given way to a blessed downpour of goodness, justice, peace, goodwill, tolerance, fraternity and empathy.

Yes, the murky age of tyranny, oppression and fanaticism, when no respect was given to freedom or good values, is over never to return. A bright dawn has broken, and the light of freedom and human rights shines forth, thanks to the upstanding men of the revolution.
Now that the times are amenable, we should take the opportunity to remember our plans to build a synagogue in Heliopolis, which is home to a considerable number of community members.

We are glad to recall that the dearly departed Rahmin Farag Lifi and the children of his late brother Ibrahim Farag donated approximately 2,000 LE as a starting fund for construction of the Heliopolis synagogue.

We should also remember that the Heliopolis Company set aside a plot of land for us to use, which we took ownership of and built walls for, and that the land comes with a specified time period within which we must begin construction or forfeit our ownership. This period has now almost elapsed.

We expended great efforts to obtain a royal decree granting permission for construction of the synagogue, knowing full well that no such decree would be forthcoming. How could permission be given to build a temple to God under a ruler known for his immorality and tyranny?

Two weeks ago, however, decrees were issued granting permission for our Christian brothers to build two temples. We live now in an era of freedom and enlightenment, and if we renew our request for permission to build the synagogue we will soon be granted our rights.
We don’t want a huge edifice which will be difficult to complete. Rather, we should start with a simple, economical design which can be expanded in future as and when finances permit.

Since this chiefly concerns the residents of Heliopolis, they should meet to discuss the matter and make a decision on building the synagogue, using their funds and efforts. When plans are underway they will receive close cooperation from the communal council and from all members of the community. Let them begin work on this project with God’s blessings.
Abu Yaʿqub

articles.title: The Greatest True Story

paragraphs.english: When I was young, I used to love reading all kinds of stories; later, I came to prefer true, real-life stories, and whenever I read a story I liked I would come to love the author more than the story itself. I loved the American writer Pearl Buck, author of {{em:The Good Earth}}, and Victor Hugo, all the more for their true-to-life stories. Once, when I was thirteen—around twenty years ago—and addicted to reading, my brother got irritated at me and scolded me loudly. Snatching my magazine away, he tore it into pieces before my eyes and shouted: “You’d better not let me catch you reading again!”

But how could I give up reading? It was an instinct in my blood that I had inherited from my mother. So I would take books out of the school library and read them in plain sight, and if my brother saw me and gave me trouble I’d show him the stamp of the school library inside the book, and he would grudgingly fall silent.

After I left school, my love of reading developed to suit my age and my circumstances. Now, I love reading the Torah, the greatest and holiest true story ever to be told on earth. The more I read it, and the better I understand its sublime meanings, the more my faith in God increases, in all my heart, all my soul, and all my might. I say that I now love Him, because previously I feared God, but I have come to love him with the love of a worshipper. The Lord our God created this book and gave it to us by the hand of Moses, His mouthpiece.

The Lord our God gave us this holy Torah for us to read, not merely to possess, and He wishes us to understand its meanings well, not to rely on traditions inherited from our ancestors without referring to the book. What this means is that we must return again and again to the Lord’s commandments, for in the Book of Deuteronomy, chapter 6 [4-9], it is written:

Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one. And thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might. And these words, which I command thee this day, shall be upon thy heart; and thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thy house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up. And thou shalt bind them for a sign upon thy hand, and they shall be for bands between thine eyes. And thou shalt write them upon the door-posts of thy house, and upon thy gates.{{fn:22}}
paragraphs.comments: [22] These verses appear in Arabic in {{em:al-Kalim}}. The English is a modified version of the Jewish Publication Society’s translation from Hebrew (1917).

paragraphs.english: The more we read the book the more clearly and easily its meanings will reveal themselves and the more our faith in it will increase. Strong faith illuminates the mind and heart, allowing humans to see things clearly and truthfully, and to distinguish good from evil.
Mrs G. L. Murad

paragraphs.english: {{em:Come with me… To the Hebrew Religious Institute at the Young Men’s Love of Torah Association}}

Spreading the Hebrew language and the message of religion is the prime concern of the businessmen and young people at the Young Men’s Love of Torah Association, who have shouldered the task of giving the children and youth of the community a religious education for free by volunteering their precious time and energy. That’s how the Association seeks to achieve its aims, and to increase its efforts it hopes that prominent and prosperous members of the community will extend a hand of assistance to help achieve its noble aspiration.
The 300 students who drink knowledge from the spring of the Association’s religious education institutes look to you and await your kindness and charity.
The Association’s institute in ʿAbbasiyyah:
1. Zaki ʿAbduh Ishaq, a student in the Faculty of Engineering and a teacher at the institute, gives a class for the youngest pupils
2. Miss Izis Hayyina. The Association is proud that one of its pupils has become a teacher, thanks to whom the girls’ section has grown and improved.
3. Students listen attentively as teacher Farag Yahuda Aslan asks a question and a female student responds.
The Association’s institute in al-Khurunfish:
1. Order is the foundation of progress. The teachers at the institute in Khurunfish instil a spirit of discipline in the youngest pupils.
2. Ili Yusif Gamil, a volunteer and member of the Association, listens attentively and affectionately to one of his female pupils at the institute in al-Khurunfish
3. This young student is confident and well prepared for his reading class.

articles.title: The Meaning of Sisit

paragraphs.english: The name {{em:sisit}} comes from the fact that the Prophet Ezekiel, peace be upon him, grew his hair long even though he was a prophet and a priest ({{em:kahin}}), as did Eliyahu, peace be upon them both; the fact they left their hair long means that it can not have been worn loose but braided, and hence their use of the words ‘the {{em:sisit}} of my head’ referred not to the hair itself but to the manner it was worn, namely braiding, and hence a sisit is only called as much if it is braided. Just as the hair is more special than the manner in which it is worn, so the {{em:hakhamim}} chose that {{em:sisit}} be made of silk, the noblest of materials; then there is the matter of who may perform it [the braiding], and in this matter our sages declared that it should be a knowledgeable person. Prayer may not be performed without the {{em:sisit}} being worn, by both males and females, and it must be worn at all times; whoever glimpses the sisit will desist from any sin they were about to commit, and the secret of that is that it reminds people of the ten commandments; a stranger may not do it, and the secret of that is that it is made of two colours: the colour white represents repentance and the colour blue represents punishment.

I—poor servant of the Lord that I am—learned to tie {{em:sisit}} and perform the requisite blessing from my late father, hakham Farag Yusif Lishaʿ, who was a {{em:hakham}}, {{em:mohel}} and {{em:shohet}}. My message here is directed to the esteemed members of the community, that they may become aware of their negligence, awaken and restore the glory of the Karaite Jews by learning the correct practice of {{em:sisit}} and its accompanying blessing, out of fear that one of the great tenets of religion might be lost. I am willing to instruct anybody, for the price of fifty piasters, provided there are at least ten people wishing to learn; I am ready to be of service. Peace be upon my esteemed fellow members of the community.
Zaki Farag Lishaʿ

articles.title: Healthy Nutrition

paragraphs.english: In a previous issue of the magazine I discussed the talented American physician Dr [Gayelord] Hauser who has earned international fame and renown for his research on the subject of healthy nutrition. As I explained, he has conducted a number of long and thorough studies that identified five nutritional substances—all widely and cheaply available—which when consumed on a daily basis in specific quantities alongside a regular diet, prevent various malnutrition-related ailments, provide immunity against other diseases, extend youthfulness, improve good looks, strengthen the health, contribute to mental serenity and stability, increase life expectancy and stave off old age. These qualities are due to the nutritional elements, vitamins, salts and acids contained in the substances in question, which are vital for a strong body and a happy, healthy life.
The five foodstuffs (which I will refer to again in future) are:
1. Yogurt, buttermilk, or similar
2. Molasses
—On the topic of the above, and their benefits, I have composed these lines of poetry:
With a bowl of yogurt at tea-time
And a spoon of molasses on top
You’ll live long and feel in fine fettle
And be sure to sleep like a rock
3. Brewer’s yeast, used in baking bread, and its dried pill derivative
4. Skimmed milk powder, i.e. milk with the fat removed which is then dried and ground
5. Wheatgerm, which is extracted from wheat by a special process
—On the topic of the latter three substances and some of their benefits, I have composed the following lines:
Take a brewer’s yeast pill every day before dinner
It’s got benefits galore, so you’re onto a winner
For health and nutrition it’s most beneficial
So incorporating it into your diet’s essential
And with dried milk powder you can’t go wrong
To improve your immunity and make you strong
Milk that’s been separated, dried and ground
It’s sure to make your constitution sound
Add a pinch to your food on every occasion
For powerful bones it’s the best foundation
Wheatgerm, too, has a splendid ability
To increase your ardor and boost your fertility
So be sure to eat well and heed my advice
It’ll nourish your health and bring you long life!
Amin al-Gamil

articles.title: Egypt’s Jews Receive Support From the Revolution

paragraphs.english: A number of high-ranking Jewish businessmen and company directors in Egypt gathered at the headquarters of the Liberation Rally for a meeting attended by minister for trade and industry Muhammad Abu Nusayr, Supreme Liberation Rally assistant secretary Ibrahim al-Tahawi, and the Rally’s director of trade union affairs Ahmad Abd Allah Tuʿayma. The officials gave speeches encouraging all Egyptian citizens to keep the interests of the nation foremost in their minds, so that its trade and commerce will flourish.
{{center:Zionism is Colonialism}}

In their speeches, the minister and Liberation Rally representatives affirmed that the revolution makes no distinction on the basis of creed and that religion is the concern of its adherents alone. They reiterated that Egypt’s struggle against Zionism is not a struggle against the Jewish faith or members of the Jewish faith, but rather a struggle against colonialism and oppression wherever they appear; and that Israel, when it attacks Egypt, attacks all Egyptians—be they Muslim, Christian, or Jew—who therefore have a right to retaliate against their aggressor.
The speakers assured all of Egypt’s Jews that they would always receive support and protection of life and property from the leaders of the revolution.
These statements were received warmly and enthusiastically by attendees who applauded at length to show their appreciation.
{{center:Solving Egyptian Jews’ Problems}}

After attendees had discussed several matters of interest to Egypt’s Jews, it was decided that a committee should be formed, chosen by concerned parties, to communicate with the leadership and cabinet and to examine and solve any problems which might arise. Attendees thanked the minister, al-Tahawi and Tuʿayma for the noble sentiments which they had expressed, and assured them of their deepest loyalty to Egypt and to its leader president Gamal Abdel Nasser.

articles.title: In the Garden of Eternity

paragraphs.english: Last Wednesday, 25th July 1956, was an ill-fated day brightened by neither sunshine nor light, for the community lost a devoted son and eminent figure. Cruel death has snatched away a tireless stalwart at a time when we need him acutely: our {{em:hakham akbar}}, our great authority Tubiyah Simhah Lifi Babufitsh.
He was a beacon who strove to guide the community to dry land, leading it ever forward so as to see it counted amongst the finest of all communities.

He came to Egypt in 1934 full of hope and aspiration, and armed with ambitious plans. No sooner had he understood the state the community was in than he took it upon himself to do everything possible to champion the weak, raise the living standards of the poor, cure the sick, and educate the ignorant. He asked the rich for their dues to the poor and the strong for their dues to the weak, having realised that in order to achieve his plans, those able to would have to pay a tithe. And so he requested tithes, thereby enacting the Lord’s commandments and our holy Torah, for example, Leviticus/Va-yiqra 27: “And all the tithe of the land, whether of the seed of the land or the fruit of the tree, is the Lord’s: it is holy unto the Lord” or Deuteronomy/Devarim 26: “When thou hast made an end of tithing all the tithe of thine increase in the third year, which is the year of tithing, and hast given it unto the Levite, to the stranger, to the fatherless, and to the widow, that they may eat within thy gates, and be satisfied…” and other verses which enjoin us to help others.

However, he was opposed by some of the community’s richer members, who waged war on his project out of fear for their wealth, which was to be reduced to nine tenths. They became angry at our {{em:hakham akbar}}, God rest his soul, for no other reason than that he asked the rich to pay their dues to the poor, and sought to enact the Lord’s commandments. They forgot that all things come to an end, “For this world is ephemeral and He the Everlasting the Eternal has power and dominion.”

Our {{em:hakham akbar}}, God rest his soul, urged us to establish a complex of endowed properties [{{em:awqaf}}] modelled on that of the Karaites in Russia, which would be a shelter for the poor and a protection for the weak, to care for them and shield them against the hardships of time. Yet most of the wealthy of the community ignored his call and only a few listened and responded, while others stopped their ears, leaving his plans to die with him.

Our great {{em:hakham}}was extremely candid. What was in his heart you would find on his lips: to one who had erred, he would say “You have erred,” and to one who had done wrong, he would say, “You have done wrong.” He knew no flattery or favouritism, often provoking the ire of his acquaintances.

He was a compassionate man who was always kind and encouraging to children before adults, saying that one must care for the young because they are the generation of the future. It was this that led him to support a number of young members of the community in establishing the institute in al-ʿAbbasiyyah in the days before the Love of Torah Association had returned to activity. Those youths will never forget the day when he came to offer his congratulations and inaugurate the institute, while others declined to attend, claiming that the young people would not be capable of sustaining an initiative which their elders had failed to keep going.

May God have mercy on you and enfold you in His grace, and inspire the community with fortitude and solace, for you were a most forbearing father and trustworthy guide, and may He recompense us with goodness for our loss.
Your son,
Z. ʿ. I
